source.title: SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoder
source.authors: Wei Shi; Zi-Yuan Xie; Sihang Li; Xiang Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE-based feature analysis can recover interpretable features in model activations, using reward-model and language-model settings rather than toy superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: Included results on human-rated or GPT-4o-rated SAE features, SAE feature visualizations, and direct feature steering. The poisoning and denoising tables are excluded because they measure downstream reward-model safety after dataset manipulation, not feature geometry or feature recovery.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK SAEs as a tool to find safety features in reward models and mainly reports its own method's poisoning and denoising performance. It assumes SAE latents are monosemantic. It reports no reconstruction, interpretability-rate or feature-distribution measure that would bear on superposition or on SAE recovery of the model's features (V4/V5). Its feature results are rater agreement, selection-versus-random comparisons, qualitative UMAP plots and steering of reward scores: related constructs, not tests of a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAFER extracts interpretable, safety-associated SAE features from reward models and that feature-guided label flipping or removal precisely degrades or improves RewardBench safety with little effect on chat. They present the steering and UMAP results as preliminary supporting evidence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses TopK SAEs trained on reward-model activations, with general-domain pretraining followed by safety-data fine-tuning; applies contrastive feature scoring, GPT-4o interpretation, UMAP visualization, and feature steering rather than testing toy-model superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that poisoning performance changes with layer position, selected feature count, dictionary size, sparsity level, and normalization constant C (Appendix A, Table 6); these are downstream manipulation results, not direct tests of feature geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: UMAP projections of SAE decoder weights show safety-related features forming separable safe and unsafe clusters across four models (qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantically related SAE features in reward and language models occupy localized regions of decoder space.

fits_no_version.finding: Amplifying SAE feature #3389 fivefold raises chosen-response reward by +1.04 on safety pairs versus +0.02 on chat pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE features exert context-selective causal influence on reward-model outputs.

record.problems: The models are described as relatively small-scale, and the authors note that evaluation on larger models remains necessary. Feature clustering evidence is qualitative, and the feature-steering evidence is preliminary, with a single feature and small samples. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these findings.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible feature-recovery or feature-geometry results were left out. Poisoning and denoising results in Tables 2–6 are omitted because they report downstream safety and chat scores after dataset manipulation rather than direct measurements of SAE feature recovery or geometry.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
No measure of features spread across neurons. No reconstruction or interpretability rate over random SAE latents; monosemanticity is assumed.
No completeness, stability or canonicity test. Dictionary-size and sparsity ablations report only downstream poisoning scores.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is an application of SAEs. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only in related work. The poisoning, denoising and ablation tables (Tables 2–6) are correctly excluded, since they measure downstream reward-model safety. The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed because no row measures V4's content.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry test.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises from competition for limited representational capacity.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.

Tests SAE-based recovery and interpretation of safety-related features, including in reward models; does not measure how features are distributed across neurons or establish prevalence across LLMs generally.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-4o and human annotators
rows.operation_detail: Compared GPT-4o and human ratings of feature safety relevance from activation contexts.

conditions.value: 500 randomly sampled from the SAE latent space

rows.measure: Absolute difference between GPT-4o and human scores
rows.value: Over 80% received identical scores (|∆| = 0); around 15% had |∆| = 1 or 2; none had |∆| > 2.
rows.note: The paper describes this as close alignment between GPT-4o and human judgments of feature safety relevance.
rows.check: Measures agreement between GPT-4o and human safety-relevance ratings. That validates the study's evaluator, not whether SAEs recover sparse features (V4).

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.size_stated: Two groups of 100 SAE features each
rows.operation_detail: Rated safety relevance of contrastively selected features and randomly sampled features.

conditions.value: SAFER-selected top-contrastive-score features versus Random features

rows.value: SAFER group concentrated near the maximum score of 5; both its mean and median scores were significantly higher than the Random group. Exact values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison, but exact score values are not given.
rows.check: Compares the study's own contrastive selection (SAFER) with random features on safety relevance. This is a method-versus-baseline selection result, not evidence on V4. No numbers are given (figure only).

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-RM
rows.operation_detail: Projected SAE decoder weights into two dimensions with UMAP and visualized safety-related features.
rows.measure: Clustering and separation of safe and unsafe features
rows.value: Safety-related features formed clear, coherent clusters; safe and unsafe features were described as distinct and separable with a well-defined local boundary.
rows.note: Qualitative visualization; no numerical clustering metric is reported.
rows.check: Qualitative UMAP of SAE decoder weights showing safe and unsafe feature clusters. This concerns topical organisation of chosen features, not superposition or recovery. No metric and no baseline.

rows.operation_detail: Multiplied the activation of safety-related Feature #3389 by a factor of 5 during reward-model scoring.
rows.note: This is a direct intervention on one SAE feature; the paper describes the feature as selectively active in safety-relevant contexts.
rows.check: Steering effect of one feature on reward scores (20 pairs). It reports no rate of feature recovery or superposition.

rows.check: Control condition for R7. A +0.02 change is the expected null for the control, so 'partial' is a mislabel. Not linked to any version.
